Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find a vector whose components correspond to the $3$rd column of the matrix $U.$
examples.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=U \Sigma V^T$ is a singular value decomposition of an $3 \times 2$ matrix $A,$ then 

- $\Sigma$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3 \times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2 \times 2$ matrix.

From the matrix $\Sigma,$ we deduce that $\sigma_1=7$ and $\sigma_2=3.$
Also, the columns $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$

Therefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute $\mathbf u_1\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{7}[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -4 & -3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{7}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{7}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{7}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute $\mathbf u_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -4 & -3 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrix $V?$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then

- $Σ$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,

- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\times 3$ matrix,

- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=3$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-9I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]-9[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -4 \\ -4 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-9I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ -4 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-1I)v=0$ gives the unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the matrix $V:$

$$
V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$
